Joint species distribution models with mvgam

Nicholas J Clark

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/articles/jsdgam.Rmd
jsdgam.Rmd

Joint species distribution models (JSDMs) assign the species co-occurrence that remains once the measured environment is accounted for to a few latent factors (Warton et al. 2015; Ovaskainen et al. 2017). The loadings imply a residual covariance among species. The factor scores ordinate the sites.

jsdgam() fits this model with the loadings identified by a QR rotation (Heaps and Jermyn 2024). This article fits it to counts of epigaeic ants at 30 sites in south-eastern Australia (Gibb et al. 2015) and adds three extensions in turn: environmental effects that act through the factors, a loadings prior informed by species traits and a prior under which the data decide how many factors are active.

The data

antTraits from the mvabund package holds counts of 41 ant species at 30 sites, five environmental covariates and five species traits. Two traits are ordinal scores, which the code below converts to numbers. jsdgam() takes one row per site and species:

data(antTraits, package = "mvabund")
abund <- antTraits$abund
# Restore the species names that make.names() mangled, such as
# "Pheidole.sp..A" for "Pheidole sp. A"
species_names <- gsub("\\.(?=\\S)", " ",
                      gsub("\\.\\.", ". ", colnames(abund)), perl = TRUE)
colnames(abund) <- species_names
env <- as.data.frame(scale(antTraits$env))
traits <- antTraits$traits
rownames(traits) <- species_names
# Pilosity and polymorphism are scores stored as unordered factors
traits$Pilosity <- as.numeric(as.character(traits$Pilosity))
traits$Polymorphism <- as.numeric(as.character(traits$Polymorphism))

ant_data <- data.frame(
  site = rep(seq_len(nrow(abund)), times = ncol(abund)),
  species = factor(rep(colnames(abund), each = nrow(abund)),
                   levels = colnames(abund)),
  counts = as.vector(as.matrix(abund))
)
ant_data <- cbind(ant_data, env[ant_data$site, ])

Because the variance of each species’ counts rises well above its mean, the counts take a negative binomial family:

moments <- data.frame(
  mean = tapply(ant_data$counts, ant_data$species, mean),
  var = tapply(ant_data$counts, ant_data$species, var)
)
ggplot(moments, aes(mean, var)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(colour = "#8F2727") +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log1p") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p") +
  labs(x = "Mean count", y = "Variance of counts")

Mean and variance of each species’ counts on log1p axes. The dashed line marks the equality a Poisson family would imply.

Latent factors alone

The first model leaves all structure among species to two latent factors. factor_formula = ~ -1 puts no covariates on the factors:

mod_base <- jsdgam(
  counts ~ 1,
  factor_formula = ~ -1,
  data = ant_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  n_lv = 2,
  unit = site,
  species = species,
  chains = 4, seed = 2025, silent = 2
)

ordinate() draws the posterior medians of the site scores and the species loadings as a biplot:

ordinate(mod_base)

Biplot of the site scores (numbered points) and species loadings (arrows) from the model with latent factors alone.

The loadings of Aphaenogaster longiceps and Crematogaster sp. A lie furthest from the origin. Their abundances vary most across sites beyond what the intercepts predict.

Environmental effects on the factors

A constrained ordination lets the environment move the sites along the factors. lv_axis() in factor_formula gives each factor its own slope on a covariate. Each species then responds to the covariate through its loadings, with two slopes per covariate in place of 41:

mod_env <- jsdgam(
  counts ~ 1,
  factor_formula = ~ -1 + Bare.ground:lv_axis() +
    Canopy.cover:lv_axis() + Shrub.cover:lv_axis(),
  data = ant_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  n_lv = 2,
  unit = site,
  species = species,
  chains = 4, seed = 2025, silent = 2
)
fixef(mod_env, trend_effects = TRUE)
#>                               Estimate Est.Error       Q2.5     Q97.5
#> Bare.ground:.trend1_trend   0.13564181 0.2762347 -0.4420674 0.6554589
#> Bare.ground:.trend2_trend   0.17603198 0.3102579 -0.4708602 0.7279889
#> .trend1:Canopy.cover_trend  0.45383186 0.5148217 -0.7700835 1.2997788
#> .trend2:Canopy.cover_trend  0.57566623 0.5925456 -0.7755250 1.4164902
#> .trend1:Shrub.cover_trend  -0.01004982 0.2378052 -0.4644986 0.4670960
#> .trend2:Shrub.cover_trend   0.08467129 0.2624600 -0.4590928 0.5574199

fixef() reports the slopes in the same rotated basis as the identified loadings Z_tilde. A species’ response is the product of its loadings and these slopes. posterior_linpred() returns it as the change in each species’ linear predictor between two sites that differ only in canopy cover:

newdata <- expand.grid(species = levels(ant_data$species),
                       Canopy.cover = c(0, 1))
newdata$site <- 1
newdata$Bare.ground <- 0
newdata$Shrub.cover <- 0
lp <- posterior_linpred(mod_env, newdata = newdata)
canopy <- lp[, newdata$Canopy.cover == 1] - lp[, newdata$Canopy.cover == 0]
canopy_q <- data.frame(
  species = levels(ant_data$species),
  t(apply(canopy, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)))
)
names(canopy_q)[2:4] <- c("lo", "med", "hi")
canopy_q$species <- reorder(canopy_q$species, canopy_q$med)
ggplot(canopy_q, aes(med, species)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = "#8F2727",
                  size = 0.25) +
  labs(x = "Response to canopy cover", y = NULL)

Posterior median and 95% credible interval of each species’ response to one standard deviation of canopy cover, on the log scale of expected counts.

The intervals of 16 of the 41 species exclude zero. The median responses run from -0.90 for Cardiocondyla nuda atalanta to 2.52 for Aphaenogaster longiceps.

Trait-informed loadings

The default prior treats every species’ loadings as independent. The traits argument replaces it with the structured prior of Heaps and Jermyn (2024). Each column of loadings is drawn from a multivariate normal whose covariance among species comes from a kernel on the standardised traits, with one length scale per trait. A short length scale lets that trait separate species’ loadings. A long one leaves them exchangeable.

mod_traits <- jsdgam(
  counts ~ 1,
  factor_formula = ~ -1,
  data = ant_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  n_lv = 2,
  traits = traits,
  unit = site,
  species = species,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  chains = 4, seed = 2025, silent = 2
)

Each length scale is named for its trait:

mcmc_plot(mod_traits, variable = "theta_features", regex = TRUE,
          type = "intervals")

Posterior medians with 50% and 90% credible intervals of the length scale of each trait.

The median length scale of Femur length, 0.28, is the shortest of the traits. It falls below the 5% quantile of 4 of the other 4 traits’ length scales. A shorter length scale gives a trait’s differences between species more weight in the loadings prior. compare_loadings() aligns the two fits’ loadings by a Procrustes rotation and draws how far each species moved:

compare_loadings(mod_base, mod_traits,
                 labels = c("uninformed", "trait-informed"),
                 label_species = "shift")

Posterior median loadings of each species without and with the trait prior, aligned to a shared basis. Labels mark the ten species that moved furthest.

Leave-one-out cross-validation compares the two priors on the same likelihood:

loo_cmp <- loo_compare(list(uninformed = loo(mod_base),
                            `trait-informed` = loo(mod_traits)))
loo_cmp
#>           model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff       diag_elpd
#>  trait-informed       0.0     0.0      NA           20 k_psis > 0.7
#>      uninformed     -30.8     8.0    1.00           21 k_psis > 0.7

Leave-one-out ranks the trait-informed prior first. The other trails it by 30.8 (SE 8.0) in expected log predictive density.

Residual correlations

residual_cor() summarises the posterior residual correlation between every pair of species. plot(cluster = TRUE) orders the species to bring blocks of co-occurring species onto the diagonal:

rcor <- residual_cor(mod_traits)
plot(rcor, cluster = TRUE)

Posterior median residual correlations from the trait-informed model. Outlined cells have 95% intervals excluding zero.

Of the 820 species pairs, 320 correlate positively and 51 negatively with intervals that exclude zero. A residual correlation may reflect a shared response to an unmeasured driver or an interaction between species. The model alone cannot tell the two apart.

How many factors?

The models so far fixed two factors. A multiplicative gamma process prior (Bhattacharya and Dunson 2011) shrinks each column of loadings more strongly than the one before. With a generous ceiling, the data decide how many columns stay away from zero. The prior combines with the trait kernel through loadings_prior:

mod_mgp <- jsdgam(
  counts ~ 1,
  factor_formula = ~ -1,
  data = ant_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  n_lv = 6,
  loadings_prior = list(column_shrinkage = "mgp", features = traits),
  unit = site,
  species = species,
  chains = 4, seed = 2025, silent = 2
)

active_factors() splits the covariance the factors give the species into principal dimensions. A dimension is active when its variance is at least a tenth of the leading dimension’s, with posterior probability of at least one half.

af <- active_factors(mod_mgp)
plot(af)

Posterior probability that each factor, largest first, is active. The dashed line marks the threshold.

In this fit, 2 of the six factors are active, against the two the earlier models fixed.

Summary

The trait prior and column shrinkage tested two assumptions of the first ant community models: independent loadings and two factors. Leave-one-out ranked the trait-informed prior first, by 30.8 in expected log predictive density against a standard error of 8.0. Given a ceiling of six factors, the shrinkage prior kept 2 active, against the two the first models assumed. Each extension is one argument to a single jsdgam() call, as are the environmental slopes that gave all 41 species a canopy response from three covariates.

Where to next

Each function used here has a help page, such as ?jsdgam, ?lv_axis or ?ordinate, with its arguments and output. how_to_cite() writes a methods paragraph for a fitted model, naming the architecture it used. jsdgam() also takes a phylogeny through phylo, trait-mediated environmental responses through trait_slopes and imperfect detection through the occ() family.

Related articles:

  • Dynamic factor models give the factors dynamics over time.
  • N-mixture models cover the closure-unit families that occ() belongs to.
  • mvgam overview introduces the observation and trend formulas.
